links.note: 791 grounds the need for inquiry on the claim that for those who keep friendship there is no leaving once it is formed (நட்டபின் வீடில்லை). 800 tells one to leave the friendship of the ஒப்பிலார், even by giving something (ஒன்றீத்தும் ஒருவுக), and Parimelazhagar takes this as the remedy for a friendship taken up unknowingly. If வீடில்லை is read as a flat 'there is no release', the two conflict; if it describes only what a true friend will not do, 800 is the exception the chapter allows.

791 says nothing ruins like befriending without inquiry (நாடாது நட்டல்), because the bond cannot be dropped afterwards. 510 says of the king's choice of men that trusting the unexamined (தேரான் தெளிவு) and doubting the one already trusted both bring endless trouble. Both put all the scrutiny before the commitment and rule out second thoughts after it, once for friends and once for officers.

791: inquire first, since after befriending there is no leaving (நட்டபின் வீடில்லை). 467: think and then resolve on a task, and to say 'we will think after resolving' (துணிந்தபின் எண்ணுவம்) is a lapse. The same order of thought before an irreversible step is applied to friendship and to action.

792 says the friendship of one who does not inquire again and again (ஆய்ந்தாய்ந்து கொள்ளாதான்) ends by giving him grief that kills him (தான்சாம் துயரம்). 508 says that trusting an outsider unexamined (தேரான் பிறனைத் தெளிந்தான்) brings trouble that does not end even down his line (வழிமுறை தீரா இடும்பை). The same warning about unexamined commitment is given for a friend and for a king's appointee, and the cost is set at one's own death in the one and at one's descendants in the other.

793 lists what to know before friendship: quality, family, fault and the person's circle (குணமும் குடிமையும் குற்றமும் குன்றா இனனும்). 504, on choosing men to trust, says to examine the qualities, examine the faults, and go by whichever is greater (குணம்நாடிக் குற்றமும் நாடி ... மிக்க கொளல்). 504 supplies the rule of decision that 793 leaves open: faults are to be known, not required to be absent, as Parimelazhagar also notes on 793.

793 includes a person's இனன், his circle, among the things to learn before befriending him (Parimelazhagar takes it as kin). 453 says that the word 'he is such a one' comes from a person's company (இனத்தானாம் இன்னான் எனப்படுஞ் சொல்). 453 gives the reason the circle belongs on 793's list: it is where a person's character is read from.

794 says the friendship of one born in a good family who is ashamed of blame on himself (குடிப்பிறந்து தன்கண் பழிநாணுவான்) should be got even by giving. 502 says trust belongs to one born in a good family, free of faults and with the shame that recoils from a blemish (குடிப்பிறந்து ... வடுப்பரியும் நாணுடையான்). Friend and king's officer are chosen by the same two marks, birth and shame at blame.

794: the friendship of the well-born man who fears blame is to be had even at a price (கொடுத்தும் கொளல்வேண்டும் நட்பு). 867 uses the same words for the opposite purchase: the enmity (பகை) of one who stays close and does unfitting things is to be had even at a price. The repeated phrase treats both the right friend and the removal of a harmful associate as worth paying for.

794 picks out as a friend the well-born person who is ashamed of blame (பழிநாணுவான்). 951 says that integrity and shame together are found by nature only in those born in a good house (இற்பிறந்தார் கண்அல்லது இல்லை ... செப்பமும் நாணும்). 951 gives the book's reason for 794 pairing birth with shame as the test.

784 says friendship is not for laughing but for going ahead to rebuke when the friend oversteps (மிகுதிக்கண் மேற்சென்று இடித்தல்). 795 turns that purpose into a rule of selection: look for and take the friendship of those able to speak so that one weeps, to rebuke (இடித்து) and to make one know what is proper (வழக்கறிய வல்லார்). What 784 defines as friendship's work, 795 uses as the test for choosing the friend.

795 says to choose as friends those who can rebuke (இடித்து) and bring one to tears over a wrong. 448 says a king without those who rebuke him (இடிப்பாரை இல்லாத) perishes even with no one to ruin him. The rebuker counts as a safeguard both for the private person choosing friends and for the king choosing his support.

796 calls ruin a rod that measures one's people to full length (கிளைஞரை நீட்டி அளப்பதோர் கோல்). 710 says the measuring rod (அளக்குங்கோல்) of those who call themselves subtle is nothing but the eye. Both use the measuring rod for finding out what people are inwardly; the courtier reads another's mind by sight, while a person's friends are only fully measured by misfortune.

796 says ruin measures out one's people (கிளைஞர்), which Parimelazhagar takes as friends. 521 says that honouring the old tie even when a man's means are gone (பற்றற்ற கண்ணும் பழைமை பாராட்டுதல்) is found only among kin. 521 states what the measuring in 796 is looking for: those who keep to the old relation after the loss.

796 says ruin shows the true length of one's friends. In 1293 the woman asks her heart whether it follows her lover on the principle that the ruined have no friends (கெட்டார்க்கு நட்டார் இல்). She is quoting a commonplace in reproach of her heart, not teaching it, but the commonplace is the one 796 assumes: most friends fall short when ruin measures them.

797 calls it gain to give up and leave the friendship of fools (பேதையார் கேண்மை ஒரீஇ விடல்). 839 uses the same phrase, பேதையார் கேண்மை, and says it is very sweet because there is no pain in parting from it. Read together, 839 is the ironic version of 797: the one good thing about such a friendship is the leaving of it.

797 counts leaving the friendship of fools as gain (ஊதியம்). 450 says that letting go the tie with the good (நல்லார் தொடர் கைவிடல்) is ten times worse than taking on the enmity of many. Whether breaking a tie is profit or harm depends on who is at the other end of it.

797 says leaving a fool's friendship is gain. 816 says that being a stranger to the wise (அறிவுடையார் ஏதின்மை) is ten million times better than close friendship with a fool (பேதை பெருங்கெழீஇ நட்பு); Pope and Subramuniyaswami render ஏதின்மை as enmity. Both verses put a fool's friendship below having no tie at all.

798 begins: do not think of what makes the spirit shrink (உள்ளற்க உள்ளம் சிறுகுவ). 596 gives the positive form: in all one thinks, think of rising (உள்ளுவதெல்லாம் உயர்வுள்ளல்). Both treat the direction of one's thoughts as something to be chosen for the sake of the spirit; 798 then sets fair-weather friends beside the shrinking thoughts as things to refuse.

798 says not to take the friendship of those who cut away in distress (அல்லற்கண் ஆற்றறுப்பார்). 106 says not to give up the friendship of those who were one's strength in sorrow (துன்பத்துள் துப்பாயார் நட்பு துறவற்க). The two prohibitions, கொள்ளற்க and துறவற்க, are complementary: how a friend behaves in trouble decides both whom not to take and whom not to drop.

798 uses ஆற்றறுப்பார் for friends who fail one in distress. 814 uses the same expression of the untrained horse that fails its rider in battle (அமரகத்து ஆற்றறுக்கும் கல்லாமா) and says solitude is better than such people as one's own. 814 supplies the picture for 798's word: support that holds until the moment it is needed.

799 says the friendship of those who abandon one in ruin burns the heart even to think of at the hour of death (அடுங்காலை உள்ளினும்). 107 says people will think, through seven births, of the friendship of those who wiped away their distress (எழுபிறப்பும் உள்ளுவர்). Both measure a friend by the memory left behind, using the same verb உள்ளு: one memory torments at death, the other is kept beyond it.

799 ends உள்ளினும் உள்ளஞ் சுடும்: even to think of the deserter's friendship burns the heart. 1207 ends with the same words in the mouth of the parted woman, for whom even remembering her lover burns. The phrase is used once for betrayal and once for separation in love; in both the pain comes from memory of a bond, not from a present injury.

799 says the thought of false friends burns the heart (உள்ளஞ் சுடும்). 293 says that after a lie one's own heart burns one (தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும்). In 293 the heart burns for one's own fault, in 799 for another's desertion, so the same inner fire is given two different causes.

800 says to stay close to the friendship of the stainless (மருவுக மாசற்றார் கேண்மை). 106 says not to forget the friendship of the stainless (மறவற்க மாசற்றார் கேண்மை). The same phrase is used in the chapter on gratitude and in the chapter on testing friends; 106 goes on to whom not to abandon, and 800 to whom one should pay to be rid of.

794 says the friendship of the well-born man who fears blame is worth getting even by giving (கொடுத்தும் கொளல்). 800 says the friendship of the ஒப்பிலார் is worth leaving even by giving something (ஒன்றீத்தும் ஒருவுக). The chapter uses the figure of payment in both directions, for acquiring a good friend and for getting free of a bad one.

800 says to leave the friendship of the unfit even at a cost. 818 says how to leave one kind of bad friend, those who make hard work of what they could do: without speaking of it, let the friendship slip (சொல்லாடார் சோர விடல்). 818 adds a manner of leaving to 800's instruction to leave.

801 defines old friendship as friendship that in no way cuts down the liberties of intimacy (கிழமையைக் கீழ்ந்திடா நட்பு). 700, on serving kings, says that the liberty (கெழுதகைமை) which does improper things on the thought 'we are old associates' (பழையம் எனக்கருதி) brings ruin. Between friends the liberty of long standing is to be accepted; with a king, presuming on it is dangerous, so 700 marks where 801's definition stops applying.

801 ties the right to take liberties (கிழமை) to பழைமை, long standing. 785 says neither meeting nor long acquaintance is needed (புணர்ச்சி பழகுதல் வேண்டா), and that shared feeling alone gives the claim of friendship (நட்பாங் கிழமை). Both use கிழமை; 785 says the claim can exist without the long acquaintance that chapter 81 takes as its ground.

802 says the liberties of intimacy are a limb of friendship and that being 'salt' to them (உப்பாதல்) is the duty of the worthy; Parimelazhagar glosses this as being pleasant toward them. 1302 says sulking between lovers is like salt in the right measure (உப்பமைந்தற்று), and too long is too much. Both use salt for what gives a relationship its taste; 1302 adds the idea of measure, which 802 does not state.

802 calls it the duty of the worthy (சான்றோர் கடன்) to take a friend's liberties well. 981 says that for those who take on worthiness knowing what is due, all good things are கடன். 802 is one instance of 981's general statement, with the same word கடன்.

803 asks what use long friendship is if one does not accept a friend's liberty as though one had done it oneself (செய்தாங்கு அமையாக் கடை). 790 says friendship looks shabby even when friends describe each other as 'they are this to us, we are that to them'. Both deny a separation of 'mine' and 'theirs' between friends: 790 in how they speak of each other, 803 in whose act an act is counted to be.

804 says that when friends act without asking, out of intimacy (கெழுதகையாற் கேளாது), it is welcomed. 788 compares friendship to the hand of a man whose garment slips, removing the distress there and then (ஆங்கே). The hand in 788 does not ask leave before acting; 804 states the same thing from the receiving side, that such unasked action is to be wanted and not resented.

797 calls it gain to leave the friendship of fools (பேதையார் கேண்மை). 805 says that when a friend does something hurtful, one should put it down either to folly (பேதைமை) or to great intimacy, which in this chapter means bearing it. Parimelazhagar separates the two by taking the folly in 805 as a passing one and not the friend's nature; on that reading 805 limits 797 to habitual fools, and old friends are excused.

805 says a hurtful act by a friend is to be understood as folly or as great intimacy (பெருங்கிழமை). 109 says that even an injury like killing is cancelled when one thinks of a single good the person did. Both teach a way of reading an injury so that the bond survives it; 109 does it by remembering a past benefit, 805 by a charitable account of the cause.

806 says those who stay within friendship's bounds do not give up the bond of those who have stood by them from of old (தொல்லைக்கண் நின்றார் தொடர்பு), even in ruin (தொலைவிடத்தும்). 521 says honouring the old tie (பழைமை பாராட்டுதல்) when a man has lost everything is found only among kin. The same constancy under loss is claimed for friends in 806 and for kin in 521; 521's 'only among kin' sits uneasily beside 806 unless true old friends are counted as kin.

806 says the bond with old friends is not given up (துறவார்) even in ruin. 106 commands: do not give up (துறவற்க) the friendship of those who were your strength in sorrow. Both use துற for abandoning a friend; 106 bases the loyalty on help received, 806 on length of standing.

807 says that those whose friendship has come by the way of love do not cut off love even when ruinous things are done to them (அழிவந்த செய்யினும் அன்பறார்). 109 says that even an injury like killing (கொன்றன்ன இன்னா செயினும்) vanishes on recalling one good the person did. Both hold that a bond can outlast grave injury from the other person; 109 names gratitude as the ground and 807 names long-standing love.

807 says old friends do not stop loving even when the friend does what brings ruin. 800 says to leave the friendship of the unfit, paying something if one must. If 800's ஒப்பிலார் includes any friend whose conduct harms one, the verses give opposite advice; Parimelazhagar avoids this by taking 800 as about a friendship entered unknowingly and 807 as about one long established in love (அன்பின் வழிவந்த கேண்மை).

808 speaks of those with the strength of intimacy not to listen to talk of a friend's lapse (கேளிழுக்கம் கேளா); Parimelazhagar takes this as not accepting it even when others report it. 510 says that doubting one who has been trusted after examination (தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவு) brings endless trouble. Both rule out reopening a settled trust, in friendship and in a king's appointments. The second half of 808 is read in opposite ways by Parimelazhagar (the day of the lapse is a day well spent) and Kalaignar (the days are wasted), so the link rests only on the first half.

187 says that those who cannot make friends by pleasant speech will divide even their own people by divisive talk (பகச்சொல்லிக் கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர்). 808 describes the friend on whom that does not work, who does not listen to reports of a friend's lapse. 187 gives the talebearer's side and 808 the hearer's refusal.

791 says that for those who keep friendship there is no leaving once it is formed (வீடில்லை). 809 says the world wants (விழையும் உலகு) those who do not leave (விடாஅர்) the friendship of friends of unbroken long standing. What 791 gives as a reason for caution before befriending, 809 presents as what earns a person general regard.

810 says those who do not depart from their nature toward old friends are wanted even by those who do not want them (விழையார் விழையப்படுப), which Parimelazhagar reads as enemies. 630 says one who takes pain as pleasure gains a distinction that even enemies desire (ஒன்னார் விழையுஞ் சிறப்பு). Both use the regard of enemies, with the same verb விழை, as the measure of a quality, constancy to friends in one and steadiness under hardship in the other.
